newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians enjoy colourful choice of candidates.
newsitem.headline: Romanians enjoy colourful choice of candidates.

text.p: Romanians voting on Sunday have a bewildering choice of colourful candidates for president, including a faith healer, a defender of motorists' rights and a defrocked priest who runs a soup kitchen.

Voters in parliamentary polls face an equally dizzying array -- 50 parties, each with its own logo, are competing. Eighteen groups represent ethnic minorities, including four Gypsy parties and six from the tiny Italian community.

The presidential contest will probably need a second round to secure a winner from the three hopefuls with any chance -- incumbent Ion Iliescu and two opposition stars, professor Emil Constantinescu and ex-prime minister Petre Roman.
Whatever the outcome the also-rans have added spice to a campaign dominated by glum statistics on growing poverty and the prospect of more belt-tightening to foster reforms.

"My power of healing comes from God. I can work miracles. I can do more than anyone else," bearded faith healer Constantin Mudava exhorted television viewers, a necklace of beads and a cross strung over his suit and tie.

Mudava, 61, earned a reputation as a healer under executed dictator Nicolae Ceausescu and says he has cured six million Romanians. His faithful must put their hands in the air and spread their legs, "to be better penetrated" by his powers.
"Whoever votes for me, votes for God," is his motto.
Nutu Anghelina, another independent, was stripped of his ministry last month by the Romanian Orthodox Church -- because he operated a network of petrol stations.
"I am financing myself as well as two soup kitchens for the poor," he said in his campaign videos.

Both men had a considerable impact on the final stages of the campaign -- embarrassed election authorities scurried to reprint six million ballots to include their missing logos -- Mudava's triangle and Anghelina's loaf of bread.
Another hopeful defending his minority -- drivers on Romania's notoriously potholed roads -- is Constantin Niculescu, head of the Motorists' Party.
"It is by no means a luxury to own a car," he told viewers. "Driving a car is a state of mind."
The most flamboyant nationalist entrant, Corneliu Vadim Tudor of the Greater Romania Party, faces 17 libel suits for articles lambasting a variety of personalities.
"I like to believe that I'm a fighter. I was born from a comsuming love," Tudor told a television interviewer, a Bible in his left hand and Romania's constitution in his right.

The nationalist Mayor of Transylvania's main city of Cluj, Gheorghe Funar, ducked a ban on the use of the red, yellow and blue national flag by appearing on television with three plastic cups on his desk -- one of each colour.

Funar has won dubious fame with diatribes against the leaders of Romania's 1.6 million-strong ethnic Hungarian minority and proposals to shorten the handles of municipal workers' picks and shovels -- so they cannot lean on them.
George Muntean, 63, the retired head of the Party of Pensioners, was magnanimous to his rivals.
"I hereby invite all the presidential candidates to join my party," he said at the end of a dreary four-hour television debate featuring all 16 hopefuls.
